extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, and cognitive scientists interested in visualization and mathematical cognition (graduate students and researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and analysis of the roles, reliability, and cognitive mechanisms of visual thinking and diagrammatic representation in mathematical practice — when visualization aids discovery, proof, understanding, or calculation and when it misleads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual thinking as heuristic aid (not final discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual thinking is a heuristic aid rather than a means of discovery: diagrams can incline a subject to certain beliefs which then must be established by proof to become knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a diagram suggesting that x·y = k never falls below x+y = 2√k and meets only on the diagonal can lead to correct algebraic inferences, but ‘‘mere attention to the diagram... cannot warrant believing’’ the required inequalities. Use visuals to generate plausible hypotheses, then supply rigorous argumentation (the visual step reduces problems to simpler algebraic manipulations). Anti-pattern: treat the diagrammatic suggestion itself as a proof without checking edge cases (e.g., extremely close intersections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations for infinite processes and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual thinking is unreliable where limits or tails of infinite processes are involved and so is rarely a means of discovery or proof in analysis involving such phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples: Weierstrass continuous nowhere-differentiable function; visual intuition about continuity/graphical crossing may fail because not all ϵ−δ continuous functions have visualizable curves. Anti-pattern: inferring global properties of infinite constructions from finite rasterizations or single-scale diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual representations to augment conceptual understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations help grasp analytically defined concepts (definitions, formulas, algorithms, operations on functions) and can make symbolically given operations more apprehensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: visualization of operations f(x)+k, f(x+k), |f(x)|, f(|x|), inverses, and integrals I(x)=∫_0^x f(t) dt; Euler's formula eiθ = cos θ + i sin θ gains geometric significance via unit circle interpretation, explaining notation reiθ, multiplicative angle-sum behaviour, and vector-length-angle interpretation. Use visuals to reveal geometric rationale behind definitions and notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualizations as explanations of definitions and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: A visual representation can explain the rationale of a definition or the aptness of a notation by making geometric or structural properties explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Euler's formula gives immediate geometric meaning to complex exponentials and explains multiplication of complex numbers in terms of lengths and angles. Use diagrams to connect algebraic laws to geometric intuition; cite Needham for further elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual thinking as a tool for discovery and proof-guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations can supply plausible conjectures and guide discovery; they can reduce a problem into simpler analytic steps that can then be proved rigorously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Computer graphics and orthogonal projections helped Hoffman and Meeks conjecture and then prove embeddedness of the Costa minimal surface. Guidance: use visual output to suggest geometry/symmetry properties and then move between images and equations to develop proofs. Anti-pattern: overtrusting computer visual evidence without analytic confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role in calculation and symbolic manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualization supports calculation by enabling rearrangement and manipulation of symbol arrays mentally or on paper; many basic algorithms are visuo-spatial in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: visual/spatial strategies underlie elementary multidigit arithmetic and matrix algebra manipulations. Note clinical correlations: visuo-spatial deficits (e.g., Williams or Turner syndromes) or agraphia (Gerstmann syndrome) can co-occur with calculation difficulties, suggesting the cognitive role of visualization in computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing discovery from proof (epistemic role of visual thinking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual thinking can be epistemically significant in leading to discovery ('seeing for oneself') even when it does not constitute a formal proof; when the visual component is non-superfluous and irreplaceable, the thinker may justifiably believe conclusions though the process might not be transparent as a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that visual insight can produce warranted belief pending formalization. One should distinguish when visual reasoning provides a reliable route to knowledge and when it merely suggests hypotheses requiring proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual template method for recognizing structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a particular visible structured set (a diagram) as a template: map elements of an external structured set onto diagram nodes and check that relations correspond (isomorphism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: name elements of the target set, label template nodes with those names, then check that labelling yields a one–one order-preserving correlation (isomorphism). This is a mechanical-perceptual task and provides epistemic access to the structure. Example: tree diagrams for parent/child relations. Scoring note: correctness depends on explicit mapping and checking; mis-identifying relevant relations (e.g., 'arrow' vs 'chain of arrows') leads to wrong template usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual category-specifications for flexible structural recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond single-instance templates, the visual system can store category-specifications (type representations) that allow recognition of diverse visual configurations as instances of the same abstract structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category specifications function like recognition patterns (analogous to face/hand recognition): activation of the stored pattern lets one see different geometrically dissimilar diagrams as the same structural kind. This supports recognizing structure without recalling a specific template. Anti-pattern: assuming conscious access to the feature-set underlying the category; category-specification is often tacit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing structure from non-visual (verbal) descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: One can recognize the structure of a verbally described set (e.g., 'Mozart, his parents, his grandparents') as isomorphic to a visual template via activation of visual category-specifications, without explicit naming/labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: cognitive access to a structure may be enabled by internal visual representations even when the stimulus is non-visual. Use this to explain quick structural analogies across domains. Anti-pattern: presuming that explicit labelling is always required to establish isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams encoding multiple operations/constants (representing richer algebraic structures)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single diagram can be construed to represent a structured set under multiple operations and constants (e.g., meet ∧, join ∨, complement −, Min/Max), yielding visual templates for algebraic structures like Boolean algebras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the cube diagram (Fig. 2.3) is a visual template for a three-atom Boolean algebra; meet/join/complement correspond to geometric relationships (e.g., complement via cube diagonals). Practice allows direct perceptual grasp of operations. Guidance: one must fix conventions mapping visual relations to algebraic operations; checking isomorphism can be done visually but requires understanding of these conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and complexity limits of visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualization is effective for small/simple structures but loses usefulness as size/complexity grows; many moderate or large algebraic structures resist helpful diagrammatic representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: drawing the power-set algebra of a four-element set becomes hard to take in and memorize; there is no easy iterative diagram-construction rule for P(n+1) from P(n). Practical guideline: prefer diagrams for small instances or for capturing essential patterns, but avoid overreliance on diagrams for large combinatorial complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual templates plus generative rules for grasping structural kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: For some structural kinds, a small set of visual templates together with simple visual rules for extending them provide cognitive grasp of the entire kind (e.g., finite discrete linear orderings with endpoints built by iteratively adding a star-line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use templates plus a clear visual operation for generating larger instances to form a visualizable species of structures (e.g., discrete linear orders, n-ary trees). This supports recognition of structural kinds beyond isolated instances. Anti-pattern: assume every structural kind admits such a generative visual rule.
